Here's why you might feel anxious when when away from your partner or support person during pregnancy, plus expert tips for how to cope with it.
Back to Top
In This Article
  • What is separation anxiety in pregnancy?
  • Why is separation anxiety so common during pregnancy?
  • How do you cope with separation anxiety in pregnancy?

Pregnancy separation anxiety, which might feel like intense fear or distress when apart from a partner or support person, can be common when you're expecting. Hormonal shifts, emotional upheaval, and the stress of impending parenthood can all contribute to symptoms. Gradual exposure to time apart, breathing exercises, and therapy may help manage symptoms before and after birth.

My husband is a big nature-loving guy. He often wakes up before sunrise and heads to the forest for a casual 9-mile hike, no big deal. So when he brought up going on an overnight backpacking trip, I was thrilled for him. Cut to the day he left for his trip: I spiraled into a full-blown panic attack, complete with shortness of breath, a racing heart, trembling, and intense fear. It was so bad I called my mom in tears.

While I'm no stranger to panic attacks, this was far from the first time my husband and I had spent time apart over the years, and it never triggered my anxiety before. But this time, things felt different, scarier, and there's one big reason — I'm pregnant with our first baby. Spending time apart from my husband for an extended period while pregnant made me feel vulnerable in a way I hadn't experienced before, which triggered fear and anxiety that lingered until he returned. 

I later learned a study found that nearly 46% of pregnant women experienced significant adult separation anxiety disorder symptoms, mostly in their third trimester. Trusted SourceNational Institutes of HealthThe Association of Dysfunctional Attitudes and Adult Separation Anxiety in Pregnancy: A Cross-Sectional StudySee All Sources [1]

So if this is something you can relate to, know that you're not alone. Keep reading to learn what experts want you to know about pregnancy separation anxiety, plus tips for coping with it. 

Key Takeaways
  • Separation anxiety during pregnancy is common. Research found that nearly half of pregnant women may experience symptoms, particularly in the third trimester.
  • Moms-to-be with separation anxiety might have headaches, disrupted sleep, panic attacks, and heart palpitations.
  • Coping strategies for separation anxiety in pregnancy include gradual exposure to time apart, deep breathing techniques, and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) if symptoms persist.

What is separation anxiety in pregnancy?

Pregnancy separation anxiety is a type of adult separation anxiety (ASA), explains Stephanie Hack, M.D., MPH, a board-certified OB/GYN. It occurs when an adult experiences intense anxiety when separated from a loved one or close attachment figure, most often a partner. 

Physical symptoms of pregnancy separation anxiety can include headaches, stomachaches, disrupted sleep, and nightmares, Dr. Hack says.

These signs can overlap with other common pregnancy symptoms, but you might also feel uncontrollable worry or angst and have thoughts like "I can't live without my partner" or "I can't do things on my own," adds Emily Guarnotta, Psy.D., a licensed clinical psychologist.

"Since becoming pregnant, I’ve gotten separation anxiety from my partner," says What to Expect Community mom 19Tyler97. "Every time he leaves, I get emotional and cry."

Like with my case, separation anxiety can also trigger panic attacks — acute episodes of severe anxiety with physical symptoms such as sweating, difficulty breathing, and heart palpitations. All of these symptoms of pregnancy separation anxiety, Guarnotta says, can lead women to avoid leaving their partner's side. 

Why is separation anxiety so common during pregnancy?

Transition periods can exacerbate separation anxiety, and pregnancy is without a doubt a life-changing transition.

"Being pregnant also sets us up for higher levels of baseline anxiety, and being separated from a support can push one over the edge," says Sipra Laddha, M.D., a reproductive psychiatrist and member of the What to Expect Medical Review Board. 

The physical, emotional, and hormonal changes women experience during pregnancy can be disorienting. That coupled with the stress of preparing for parenthood can make expectant moms more vulnerable to experiencing mood or anxiety disorders. 

Women who experience anxiety during pregnancy are also more likely to experience anxiety postpartum as well."These hormonal changes combined with sleep deprivation and the demands of caring for a newborn can contribute to developing postpartum separation anxiety," Guarnotta says. 

How can you cope with separation anxiety in pregnancy?

Gradually ease into time apart

Expose yourself to what makes you anxious, such as spending time away from your support person, suggests Dr. Hack. The key is to do it gradually, starting with short periods and increasing the length of time as you feel more comfortable.

Most importantly, do not avoid what makes you anxious, as it only reinforces anxiety. Though it may give you some temporary relief to avoid a trigger, avoidance typically worsens overall anxiety levels in the long run, Dr. Laddha says.

Learn and practice deep breathing skills

Breathing deeply can help ease your symptoms when anxiety arises. "Deep breathing can get more oxygen into your body and activates the parasympathetic nervous system, which helps you recover from the fight-or-flight response," Guarnotta says. "To do this, take a four-second long inhale through your nose, hold, and then release the air through your mouth for six seconds."

Get help if symptoms persist 

Lastly, seek support from a therapist if needed. Therapy can get to the root of the separation anxiety, Guarnotta says. Specifically, she recommends cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), which can modify unhealthy beliefs contributing to separation anxiety. Getting support during pregnancy means you'll learn how to cope with separation anxiety if it occurs after birth as well. 

If you're experiencing pregnancy separation anxiety, remember that you're not alone in your experience. Don't hesitate to reach out for support from loved ones or professionals when needed. 

As for me, talking to my therapist and doubling down on self-care to soothe my nervous system has been a big help. I'm happy to report I entered my third trimester feeling much more empowered and at ease.

Pregnant in the heat? Don't be surprised if you develop heat rash. Here's what it looks like and how to relieve the itch.
Back to Top
In This Article
  • What are the symptoms of heat rash during pregnancy?
  • What causes heat rash during pregnancy?
  • How do I treat heat rash during pregnancy?
  • What remedies don’t work for pregnancy heat rash?
  • When should I see a doctor about heat rash during pregnancy?

Heat rash looks like tiny bumps, bug bites, or pimples. You may have seen it on babies, but it's also very common during pregnancy. Wearing light, loose clothing and keeping cool with air conditioning, cool or tepid baths, and cool, wet washcloths can soothe the itch of this annoying skin condition.

Learn more about why heat rash happens during pregnancy and what you can do about it.

Key Takeaways
  • Heat rash is common during pregnancy and is caused by trapped sweat. Pregnancy can increase body temperature and make you sweat more, which can clog sweat ducts and lead to small red or pink bumps that may itch or sting.
  • Keeping cool and reducing friction are the best ways to treat and prevent heat rash. Loose cotton clothing, cool compresses, tepid baths, fans, and air conditioning can reduce itching and help the rash heal. Calamine lotion and talc-free powders may also provide relief.
  • Most heat rashes are harmless, but persistent or severe symptoms should be checked by a doctor. See your doctor if the rash lasts more than a few days, becomes painful, shows signs of infection, or is accompanied by other concerning symptoms.

What are the symptoms of heat rash during pregnancy?

Science Source; iStock

Heat rash appears as pink or red, bug-bite-like bumps that can itch or feel prickly or sensitive. It can sometimes look like pimples and may even develop whiteheads. Trusted SourceMayo ClinicHeat RashSee All Sources [1]

You're most likely to see it in areas where sweat becomes trapped between the folds of your skin, such as:

  • In the creases between and beneath the breasts
  • Where the bulge of the lower abdomen rubs against the top of the pubic area
  • On your back
  • On the inner thighs
  • On the armpits
  • In the creases of your elbows

"I get heat rashes a LOT when pregnant!" says What to Expect Community member eclaire24. "Often on my thighs or under my boobs."

It can easily be confused with with other pregnancy-related skin conditions, such as:

  • Hives, or itchy, raised welt-like bumps that can appear suddenly on the body, usually as an allergic reaction. Hives tend to last anywhere from a few days to a few weeks.
  • Prurigo, which often appears as itchy, crusty bumps on your arms or legs, and can happen at any point in pregnancy.
  • Pruritic folliculitis, which causes acne-like, pus-filled bumps that may appear on your torso and spread to your arms, chest, and back. It typically develops during the second trimester or third trimester.
  • Pemphigoid gestationis, which is a rare autoimmune skin disorder that can suddenly pop up in the second or third trimester and cause a hive-like rash on your midsection that can turn into blisters.
  • Cholestasis of pregnancy, which is an intense itch all over your body, particularly on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. It typically shows up in the third trimester and may be accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and jaundice (the whites of the eyes and skin may be yellow-colored). Cholestasis is not actually a rash — it's a sign of liver disease triggered by your hormones and should be evaluated by a doctor.
  • Pustular psoriasis of pregnancy, which is a severe form of pustular psoriasis that appears as red, inflamed, crusty lesions — commonly on the thighs and groin — during the second half of pregnancy.
  • Pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy (PUPPP), which appears as itchy, red, raised skin patches on the stomach, often near stretch marks, and can spread to your limbs. PUPPP typically only develops in your first pregnancy, during the third trimester.

What causes heat rash during pregnancy?

Also known as prickly heat, heat rash happens when the sweat ducts in your pores become clogged, trapping perspiration beneath the skin. It tends to crop up during the hot, humid months.

Heat rash can be triggered by a combination of pregnancy-related changes: increased body heat, excessive perspiration, and friction from skin rubbing against itself or clothing. While it's not pretty, fortunately prickly heat is usually only slightly irritating.

"I am very prone to heat rash normally, so I expected it in pregnancy," says Community mom BoyMomEst2023. "But it came on so much faster than usual!"

How do I treat heat rash during pregnancy?

Wondering how to beat the heat? There are plenty of pregnancy-safe ways to soothe itchy skin and help heal your heat rash.

  • Wear light, loose-fitting cotton clothes. To help minimize sweating and friction, avoid tight-fitting clothing and leggings. And choose your fabrics wisely — synthetic material can worsen sweating, and scratchy ones like wool can cause itching.
  • Apply a cool, damp compress to your skin. To cool the rash, try soaking a washcloth in cold water or chilled green tea and applying it to the affected area for five minutes, three times a day.
  • Rinse off. Take warm or tepid (not hot) baths and showers — and don't linger for too long, use harsh soaps, or make the water too hot. A tepid oatmeal bath can also be very soothing, as oatmeal contains compounds that relieve inflammation.
  • Pat on powder. Sprinkle a bit of cornstarch or talc-free powder to absorb sweat during the day.
  • Apply calamine lotion. It contains zinc oxide, which has soothing properties and can temporarily relieve itching as it dries.
  • Turn on the air conditioning or a fan. This can help you avoid overheating, stay cool, and keep sweat at bay.
  • Get naked. And stay that way whenever you can. Fresh air is the best antidote to heat rash.
  • Ask your doctor about hydrocortisone cream. Many over-the-counter heat rash remedies contain hydrocortisone, a common anti-itch ingredient. But before you apply the medication, check with your dermatologist or pharmacist to make sure the ingredients are safe to use during pregnancy.

"It was behind my knees and in my elbow crease," says Community mom OnlyaGeniousCouldLoveMe. "I used hydrocortisone cream. Went away in about a week and a half. No issues ever since!"

What remedies don't work for pregnancy heat rash?

You should steer clear of some treatments and products when you have heat rash during pregnancy, including:

  • Skin irritants. Stay away from perfumes, fragranced lotions, and harsh soaps.
  • Petroleum-based ointments or mineral oil creams. Heavy creams or oils can worsen heat rash because they may further block sweat ducts.

When should I see a doctor about heat rash during pregnancy?

Usually, heat rashes are harmless. But there are certain symptoms that may warrant a call to your doctor, including:

  • If the rash or irritation lasts longer than a couple of days.
  • If you're experiencing pain or intense itching.
  • If the rash becomes infected — for example, it leaks pus or fluid, or is accompanied by symptoms like swelling, fever, and nausea.

While it may not be pretty or comfortable, in all likelihood, your heat rash will fade within a few days — and be nothing more than a mild inconvenience.


Heat Rash During Pregnancy FAQs

How do you treat heat rash during pregnancy?

You can treat heat rash during pregnancy by taking a warm, tepid, or cool bath, staying in a cool, air-conditioned room, and applying a cool damp washcloth soaked in cool water or green tea to the area three times a day for about five minutes at a time.

What does heat rash look like?

Heat rash appears as clusters of tiny red, pink, or clear bumps on the skin that are often itchy or feel prickly. Heat rash can look like small bug bites or pimples.

How long does heat rash last when you're pregnant?

Heat rash usually disappears on its own, whether you're pregnant or not, and typically won't last more than a few days. If you've had heat rash for longer than three days, call your practitioner.

Does heat rash spread?

No, heat rash isn't contagious and doesn't typically spread, though you can exacerbate the rash by scratching it too much or using lotions, oils, or powders.
